q: Should a franchisor count its franchisees' purchases, like ingredients, in Scope 3?
title: Franchisee purchases in franchisor Scope 3
short: Yes, when they are significant. The minimum for Category 14 is your franchisees' Scope 1 and 2. The GHG Protocol's calculation guidance adds that a franchisor should include significant upstream emissions from what franchisees buy, and gives the example of a fast-food chain and the beef its restaurants purchase.
audience: Franchisors in food, retail and services, and their sustainability teams

p: Category 14 applies to franchisors. Its minimum boundary is the Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions of franchisees while they run the outlets: grid power, DG set diesel, kitchen LPG or PNG, refrigerant top-ups. The emissions from building or fitting out the outlets are optional.

The Technical Guidance goes one step further than the minimum: if significant upstream emissions result from goods and services that franchisees buy, the franchisor should include them in Category 14. Its example is a large fast-food franchise counting the upstream emissions of the beef its restaurants buy.

The same chapter lists franchisees' own Scope 3 data as optional to collect. Read the two together: you need not gather every franchisee's full Scope 3, but a large source such as meat, dairy or cooking oil bought by every outlet should be counted.

sections.h: Do not count the same kilo twice
ul: If your central kitchen or warehouse buys the ingredient and supplies it to outlets, its upstream emissions are already in your Category 1 when you buy it. Leave it out of Category 14.
Count in Category 14 only what franchisees buy directly, for example from your approved vendors.
Franchisee travel, waste and packaging they buy locally can stay out unless they are large for your business; say what you left out and why.

ol: If you mandate approved vendors, ask them for quantities supplied per outlet per month. One report from a vendor beats a hundred franchisee replies.
Otherwise ask franchisees for kilograms or litres by item from their purchase invoices, not costs.
With many outlets, the guidance allows a representative sample, grouping outlets of similar type and size, then scaling up.
Multiply quantities by a cradle-to-gate factor per kilogram for each item, and state the factor source.

example.title: Illustration: 120 franchised outlets of a chicken restaurant chain
lines: Outlet power: 120 x 4,000 kWh a month x 12 = 57,60,000 kWh x 0.675 = 3,888 t CO2 (minimum boundary)
Chicken bought direct from approved vendors: 120 x 900 kg a month x 12 = 12,96,000 kg, or 1,296 t
At an assumed 5 kg CO2e per kg: 1,296 x 5 = 6,480 t CO2e
Leaving purchases out would report 3,888 t when the larger source is 6,480 t
example.note: Outlet power and chicken quantities are illustrative, and 5 kg CO2e per kg is a placeholder chosen to show the method, not a published factor; use a cited factor for your sourcing region. 0.675 is the India grid factor for FY 2025-26 (CEA version 22.0).

senseible: Senseible reads the electricity bills, LPG invoices and approved-vendor purchase invoices that franchisees share, and keeps purchase lines in a separate supplier evidence trail, so outlet energy and ingredient quantities stay apart and each traces to its document.

sources.label: GHG Protocol Technical Guidance for Calculating Scope 3 Emissions, Category 14: Franchises
